newsitem.title: UK: Turkey walks fiscal tightrope, London analysts say.
newsitem.headline: Turkey walks fiscal tightrope, London analysts say.

text.p: Turkey may risk a crisis next year with speculative attacks on the country's currency if its precarious fiscal situation does not improve, several analysts in London said.

"In the worst-case scenario...the public-sector borrowing requirement would rise to unsustainable levels and a balance-of-payments crisis could ensue," said Susanne Hallergard, economist at ING Barings. "A crisis could come as early as March."
She said the government currently spends nearly 55 percent of its revenues on interest payments and that could jump to 70 percent without fiscal cutbacks and a more realistic budget.

Others said the malaise was having an impact on the entire economy. "The economy is utterly out of kilter and has largely become uncompetitive," said one London-based analyst, who declined to be named.
"There is too much imported inflation, and there is too little export growth," he added.
Analysts said the government was pursuing a policy of high spending with a short-term strategy of generating higher revenues through privatisation.
An International Monetary Fund (IMF) delegation will visit in January after having expressed reservations about the government's plans during its last visit in October.

Turkey's inflation rate is currently more than 80 percent on an annualised basis. Its economy has also been growing rapidly, with real 1996 gross domestic product growth projected near eight percent, but this has come from domestic demand rather than trade-driven growth, analysts said.
Turkey would likely hold elections by mid-1997, and possibly sooner if the lira faced speculative attacks, the unnamed London-based analyst said.

He said the currency, which has steadily appreciated in inflation-adjusted terms against the dollar since it was devalued 30 percent in 1994, risked reaching unsustainable levels where it would be dangerously exposed.

The wildly optimistic 1997 budget presented by Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's government, which claimed it would balance the budget in 1997 after an expected gap of nine percent of GDP in 1996, was particularly troubling, analysts said.

Turkey's long-term foreign currency debt is rated Ba3 by Moody's and B-plus by Standard and Poor's. Both rating agencies have placed the country on credit watch. Analysts uniformly brushed off as unrealistic the government's forecasts, which relied heavily on projected privatisation revenues of nine billion dollars, an estimate which the Prime Minister raised to $13 billion last week.
"There is no way they can reach that level," Hallergard said.
They expected 1997 receipts of around three billion dollars.
Some analysts, however, disagreed that a crisis was looming and believed Turkey could ride out any problems.
"I'm not expecting any financial or currency crisis," said Deborah Bennellick, economist at UBS. "Turkey is much stronger than people had been expecting."
Analysts said the current coalition between the Islamic-oriented Refah Party and the center-right True Path Party had proven surprisingly stable.
"A fiscal crisis can easily be avoided if the government even partially achieves its targets," said Michael Harris, equity analyst at Merrill Lynch.
Analysts also said Turkey still had some attractive investment opportunities, particularly in equities.

Relative to other emerging markets, Turkish equities look cheap with a price earnings multiple of eight times 1996 earnings, analysts said. But because of market volatility, it was difficult to estimate the appropriate risk premium.
"The risk premium is overblown, Harris said. "There is a window of opportunity here."
